summary: Flame Atlas is a fully sourced evidence base and website that turns NASA’s microgravity fire experiments into an answer to one question for future lunar habitats: in Moon Base air (30% oxygen or more at 10.2 psi or less), does turning off the fans still put out a fire? It brings together 30 investigations, 895 tests and 69 sources from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) system, NASA reports and published papers, and ties every value to a quote from its source. The site maps 881 tests by oxygen and pressure, ranks 28 investigations by how directly they bear on the question, records errors found in NASA’s data files, and has an AI Ask box in which Claude answers only from the verified records and cites its sources. Our reading of the evidence is “not reliably”: in normal air, cutting the airflow usually put flames out, but with more oxygen flames lasted longer and many kept burning with no airflow at all. This matters because cutting ventilation is an established step in fighting spacecraft fires, and the BASS-II research team has noted that this step “may not be applicable in future exploration missions
details:
What it does:
Flame Atlas gathers NASA’s microgravity combustion data into one evidence base built around a practical question for lunar habitats: in Moon Base air (30% oxygen or more at 10.2 psi or less), does turning off the fans still put out a fire? The site has five parts:

  • Evidence base: 30 investigations, 895 tests and 69 sources. Every value (oxygen, pressure, airflow, burn time, outcome) is tied to a verbatim quote from its source, with the page or line.
  • Moon Base map: 881 tests plotted by oxygen and pressure (14 others lack one of the two), with filters. 23 fall inside the Moon Base zone and 17 at its edge.
  • Ask box, the project’s SI component: Claude Sonnet 5.5 answers visitors’ questions using only the verified records and cites the investigation, source and page. Each visitor gets 10 questions a day. If the API is unavailable, the box falls back to five hand-checked answers.
  • Rankings: 28 investigations ranked by how directly they inform the fans-off question, each with its reason and evidence.
  • Data problems: errors found in NASA’s own files, recorded as caveats rather than silently fixed.

What we found:
Our reading of the evidence is “not reliably.”

  • In normal air, cutting the airflow usually put flames out. In BASS-II (up to 22.2% oxygen), flames always quenched when the fan was turned off. In ACME BRE, every flame in normal air (21% oxygen, 14.7 psia) went out on its own within 40 s.
  • With more oxygen, flames lasted longer and many kept burning with no airflow. In ACME BRE at 27% oxygen and 10.2 psia, and at 34% and 8.2 psia (inside the Moon Base zone), flames generally persisted 3 minutes or more; one 27% flame went out at 45 s. None of 17 FLEX droplet flames at the zone’s edge went out on its own.
  • How the airflow is cut may matter. In Saffire V, acrylic samples went out at once when the fan was turned off after 5 minutes of reduced airflow, but a cotton fire grew back when the fan restarted after 70 s off. The authors conclude that extinguishment of thin charring fuels at increased oxygen “cannot be assumed to occur rapidly in quiescent conditions.”
  • The key gap: no test we found turned the airflow off on real cabin materials inside the Moon Base zone.

How it works:

  • Data: Claude read NASA PSI experiment tables, metadata files and PDF reports, and extracted each value with a verbatim quote and its page or line. A Python build script checks the quotes against the source files: 3,115 matched word for word, and 13 table rows were checked cell by cell. Problems in the sources are recorded as caveats instead of being silently fixed.
  • Human check: we checked 30 values by hand against the original files (20 random tests and 10 headline claims). All 30 were found and 29 matched. The other was a value the source never stated, and it is now marked “not stated.” The check also found seven overstatements, which were rewritten, and a conflict between two tables in a NASA report. Five Ask-box answers were reviewed by hand, and one figure was corrected.
  • Accuracy test: to see whether AI can read NASA’s raw tables reliably, Claude Haiku 5.5 extracted five values per test from 8 PSI tables (881 tests) on its own. Scored against a hand-verified answer key, it got 3,096 of 3,104 values right (99.7%), and 98.5% on a repeat run. Counting values the sources leave ambiguous, the scores are 96.6% and 95.3%. Against the original, uncorrected key they are 95.0% and 93.6%. Every run and correction is published in the repository.
  • Site: built in Framer. The Moon Base map and Ask box are React code components that load the data from GitHub through jsDelivr. The Ask box calls a Node.js serverless function on Vercel, which sends the question and a digest of the verified records to Claude Sonnet 5.5.

Who it helps:
Habitat and life-support engineers deciding how crews should respond to a fire in high-oxygen, low-pressure air. Fire-safety researchers looking for which experiments exist near Moon Base conditions and which are missing. Anyone who needs a claim traced to the exact NASA page it came from.

What we hope to achieve:
To make “fans off” a question answered with evidence before it goes into lunar-habitat procedures. The next experiments we recommend are:

  • fans-off tests on real cabin materials inside the Moon Base zone
  • tests in lunar gravity
  • measurements of how smoke reaches detectors when the fans are off

We also hope the data problems we found help NASA correct its records.

Tools:

  • Python: data build, quote checks and accuracy test
  • Node.js with the Anthropic SDK: Ask API
  • React and TypeScript: Framer code components
  • Framer: website
  • Vercel: API hosting
  • GitHub and jsDelivr: code and data hosting
  • Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Ask box), Claude Haiku 5.5 (accuracy test), and Claude and Claude Code (data extraction, code and writing)

Code and data: https://github.com/R-Nour/Flame-Atlas
